notes.meaning: Judah's plea broke Joseph's heart, and he could no longer hold back his deep love for his family. He ordered all his Egyptian attendants to leave the room so he could speak with his brothers in private. He did this out of kindness, to protect his brothers from being shamed in front of strangers for their past crime.
Joseph cried so loudly that the Egyptian servants outside the room could hear his deep weeping. Word of his loud crying spread quickly until it reached Pharaoh's royal palace.

Joseph revealed his true identity to his brothers and asked if his father was really still alive. His brothers were so shocked and terrified that they could not speak a word. They were frozen in fear, realizing the ruler before them was the very brother they had wronged.

Seeing how frightened his brothers were, Joseph gently invited them to step closer to him. He repeated his name and reminded them that he was the brother they had sold into Egypt. He named what they had done not to hurt them, but to prove who he was and prepare them for mercy.

Joseph told his brothers not to torment themselves with grief or anger over selling him. He explained that God had sent him ahead of them to save lives from the famine. When people harm us, God can still use the outcome to work out His good purposes.

Joseph explained that the severe famine had already lasted two years. There were still five years to come in which no crops could be plowed or harvested. This left the land without food and made God's help urgently necessary.

God sent Joseph ahead of his family to preserve a remnant, which means a surviving line of descendants on the earth. Through this great rescue, God kept His covenant promises to Abraham and Jacob from being cut off.

Joseph insisted that God was the true mover behind his arrival in Egypt, rather than the brothers' wicked deed. God had raised him to be a trusted advisor to Pharaoh and the ruler of all Egypt to rescue people from death.

differ.view: God did not merely permit the brothers' sinful action, but actively directed their evil deed toward His good rescue plan while leaving the moral guilt entirely on them.

notes.meaning: Joseph urged his brothers to hurry back to Canaan with the good news for their father. They were to tell Jacob that God had made Joseph lord of all Egypt and that he should come down without delay.
Joseph offered the fertile land of Goshen as a home for his father, brothers, children, and livestock. Living there would place them close to Joseph, where he could protect and care for them.
Joseph promised to feed and care for the whole family during the five remaining years of famine. If they stayed in Canaan, their food and herds would run out, leaving them ruined.

Joseph pointed out that they could see his face and hear his voice speaking to them in their own Hebrew tongue without an interpreter. Benjamin especially could witness that this powerful ruler was truly their lost brother.
Joseph instructed his brothers to tell their father about his great honor in Egypt and all they had witnessed. He told them to hurry and bring his father down so they could be reunited.
Joseph embraced his younger brother Benjamin and wept openly, and Benjamin wept in his arms. Having the same mother, Rachel, the two brothers shared a deep bond of love and relief.

Joseph kissed and wept over each of his other brothers as a sign of complete forgiveness and peace. Only after these warm embraces were the brothers able to overcome their fear and talk freely with him.

When the news reached Pharaoh's palace that Joseph's brothers had arrived, the king and his court were genuinely pleased. Because Pharaoh valued Joseph so highly for saving the nation, he welcomed Joseph's family with open arms.
Pharaoh officially commanded Joseph to send his brothers back to Canaan with loaded pack animals. The king gave royal authority and support to Joseph's desire to care for his family.
Pharaoh promised to give Jacob and his family the best land in Egypt and the finest food the country could produce. He wanted to honor Joseph by treating Joseph's family like royal guests.

Pharaoh told them to take royal Egyptian transport wagons back to Canaan to carry the young children, wives, and their aging father. These wheeled carriages would make the rough, long trip manageable for the weak and elderly.
Pharaoh told them not to worry about any heavy household goods they might have to leave behind in Canaan. The finest possessions and resources of all Egypt would belong to them once they arrived.
The sons of Jacob obeyed the king's orders. Joseph gave them wagons as Pharaoh commanded, along with plenty of food and supplies for their journey.

Joseph gave each brother a new set of fine clothing, but he gave Benjamin five changes of clothes and three hundred pieces of silver. This special gift showed his unique affection for his full brother, and the other brothers accepted it without jealousy.

Joseph sent twenty donkeys loaded with Egyptian delicacies, grain, bread, and supplies to his father Jacob. These generous gifts served both to feed his father on the journey and to prove Joseph's wealth and devotion.

As Joseph sent his brothers away, he warned them not to quarrel or argue on the road home. Knowing their history, he wanted to prevent them from blaming one another for selling him into slavery now that he had forgiven them all.
The brothers traveled up from the lowlands of Egypt and arrived safely at their father Jacob's home in Canaan.

The sons told Jacob that Joseph was still alive and ruling over all Egypt, but the sudden news overwhelmed him. Jacob's heart went cold with shock, and he could not bring himself to believe what sounded impossible.

The brothers repeated everything Joseph had told them, and Jacob saw the Egyptian wagons sent to transport him. The sight of these tangible proofs broke through his doubt, and his fainting spirit came back to life.
Jacob declared that hearing his son Joseph was alive was all he needed to know. His faith and strength were renewed, and he resolved to travel to Egypt to see Joseph with his own eyes before he died.
